props.title: The update loop, and one clever trick
lines: for f in F:                               # each candidate fact
op = classify_operation(f, M)         # the LLM decides
if op == UPDATE: m = related(f, M)
# the LLM sees ids "0","1","2", never UUIDs

notes.t: classify each fact against its neighbours
UPDATE only if the new fact carries more information
UUIDs → short integers: fewer copying errors
JSON out: id, text, event, old memory

props.sub: DELETE is irreversible in the store · the history table is the only undo

captions: Part four. Phase two: update. This is where
the memory stays consistent.
Each candidate fact is handled on its own.
First it's embedded, and the vector store returns
the ten most similar existing memories.
The fact and those neighbours go to the
LLM through a function call. The paper calls
it a tool call.
The LLM picks one of four operations. ADD,
when nothing equivalent exists. UPDATE, when the fact
enriches an existing memory. DELETE, when it contradicts
one. And NOOP, when it's already known, or
irrelevant.
There's no separate classifier. The LLM's own reasoning
makes the decision.
Let's run it on a real sequence.
Riya says she lives in Pune and loves
cricket. Two ADDs.
She gives her name. Another ADD.
Later she says she's moved to Bengaluru. That
contradicts the Pune memory, so it's deleted, and
the new city is added.
She adds that she especially loves Test matches.
That enriches an existing memory, so it's an
UPDATE.
And when she repeats that she loves cricket,
nothing changes. NOOP.
Every step is also written to a history
table, so you can see how each memory
evolved.
Here's the logic from the paper's Algorithm One.
For each fact, classify the operation. An UPDATE
only replaces the old memory if the new
one carries more information.
Now, one clever implementation detail. Memory ids are
long UUIDs, and LLMs are bad at copying
them exactly. So before the prompt, Mem0 maps
them to short integers, zero, one, two, and
maps them back afterwards.
The model returns JSON: an id, the new
text, the event, and the old memory, for
the audit trail.
A cheap trick, with a big reliability win.
There's a risk hiding in this design.
An LLM decides what to forget. If it
misreads a sarcastic remark, or a hypothetical, it
can delete a true memory.
LLM decisions also vary from run to run,
so the same conversation can produce slightly different
memory stores.
The history table is the safety net: every
change is recorded, so a bad delete can
be audited, and undone.
Keep this risk in mind. It's one reason
the design changed in twenty twenty six.
